text:
A common assumption is that the mental health side of menopause comes later, after the hot flushes, and is mostly about falling oestrogen. The evidence points somewhere more useful. Perimenopause, the transition before the final period, is when the likelihood of depressive symptoms rises compared with the premenopausal years, and mood, anxiety and cognitive changes can arrive years before hot flushes.

The leading explanation is not simply lower oestrogen but how unpredictably it fluctuates. Some women are more sensitive to these shifts, and that sensitivity is amplified by recent stressful life events. A history of premenstrual dysphoric disorder or postnatal depression, past depression, current stress and disrupted sleep are consistent risk factors. Midlife brain fog is common and, in almost all cases, is not an early sign of dementia.

ADHD is a newer strand. Oestrogen modulates dopamine, which is central to the attention systems ADHD already involves, offering a plausible reason some women notice ADHD traits feeling more pronounced in midlife. Women with ADHD report higher perimenopausal symptom burden, and midlife is a common point of first recognition, which can mean gaining language for a lifelong experience.

Menopause-specific cognitive behavioural therapy has guideline-level support for mood, sleep and the distress linked with hot flushes. Guidelines support considering menopause hormone therapy for some people, a conversation to have with a medical practitioner.

What this might mean in practice, whatever your role:
• Ask gently and directly. Many women do not link changes in mood, focus or organisation to the transition, or feel able to raise them.
• Notice symptoms that emerge suddenly in midlife and fluctuate, and ask about sleep alongside mood.
• Involve a GP when midlife mood, sleep or attention changes appear, and respond promptly to any disclosure of thoughts of self-harm.

Where the evidence stops:
• No controlled studies have yet examined ADHD during menopause. The change many women describe rests on clinical observation and mechanism for now.
• ADHD findings are not uniform. One study did not find worse symptom perception at every stage.
• Anxiety, and the experiences of culturally diverse and First Nations Australian women, are less studied than depression.
• Hormone therapy is not established as a first-line treatment for diagnosed major depressive disorder.
